summary:
What we developed: ASTRA Companion is an offline-first astronaut health and well-being platform for long-duration Moon and Mars missions. It integrates three parts: an astronaut-facing app with a deterministic AI companion (mood check-ins, guided breathing, voice interaction), a health intelligence engine that compares vital signs and dosimeter readings against personal baselines to surface explainable risks, and a Ground Station dashboard for Earth-side medical teams. Supporting it are a signed-data Hub, a link simulator for delays and outages, encrypted backups, and a scenario evaluation harness backed by 96 Python/Companion tests, 21 UI tests, and Playwright smoke tests.

How it addresses the challenge: Instead of fixed thresholds and physical readings alone, ASTRA tracks trends, blends physical and psychological well-being, and keeps working in Autonomous Mode when Earth contact is lost — showing the Ground Station exactly how stale its last-received data is.

Why it matters: Protection of crews on deep-space missions cannot depend on real-time connectivity or reactive diagnosis. ASTRA turns monitoring into continuous, personalized decision support — and treats the astronaut as a whole person, not a stream of numbers.
details:
What it does and how it works

ASTRA Companion is an offline-first astronaut health and well-being platform for long-duration Moon and Mars missions. It runs as six cooperating services: an Astronaut App, an AI Companion, a health evaluation engine, a Ground Station for Earth-side flight surgeons, a signed-data Hub, and a Link Simulator that reproduces delay, disconnection, and store-and-forward behavior.

Wearable and dosimeter readings are signed and ingested by the Hub, then compared against each astronaut's personal baseline — not fixed population thresholds. The engine uses robust statistics (median/MAD), EWMA baseline adaptation, rolling windows, and persistence checks, so a single odd reading does not raise an alarm. It correlates multiple signals (e.g., falling sleep + rising resting heart rate + falling mood), handles radiation dose-rate and cumulative-dose budgets, tracks post-exposure follow-up windows, and distinguishes a sensor fault from a real physiological change. Alerts carry plain-language reasons, a confidence score, a decision level, and a recommended action.

The Companion provides deterministic mood check-ins, stress/energy self-assessment, alert explanations, breathing/grounding exercises, and optional local voice (Vosk speech-to-text, Piper text-to-speech). It deliberately uses no LLM or cloud calls, so it is auditable, fast, and available with no internet. Crisis language triggers a fixed supportive script and escalation to a flight psychologist.

When the Earth link drops, the Astronaut App continues in Autonomous Mode; queued messages sync on reconnection by priority (urgent health and security traffic is never rate-limited). The Ground Station always labels data as live or last-received, with its age.

Benefits

  • Whole-person monitoring — physical vitals, sleep, mood, and radiation in one system.
  • Fewer false alarms — personal baselines, persistence, and multi-indicator logic.
  • Psychological support exactly when isolation is worst, without connectivity.
  • Explainable decision support rather than opaque scores or diagnoses.
  • Security by design — Ed25519 signatures, AES-GCM field encryption, Argon2 password hashing, short-lived JWTs, role-based access, and an append-only audit chain.

Intended impact

ASTRA targets the operational reality of deep-space medicine: no real-time link, no hospital, and months of cumulative risk. It aims to give crews earlier, calmer awareness of health drift and give Earth-side teams trustworthy, time-stamped context even after an outage. It is a decision-support prototype intended to grow into an analog-mission and remote-medicine platform with validated medical references.

Tools and technology

  • Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, SQLite, cryptography (Ed25519, AES-GCM), PyJWT, Argon2, SlowAPI, WebSockets.
  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite 6, React Router 7, Recharts, lucide-react, MSW for fixture mode, npm workspaces with shared contract/UI packages, and JSON Schema → TypeScript type generation.
  • Voice: local Vosk (STT) and Piper (TTS) models, processed in memory, never stored or uplinked.
  • Quality/security: pytest, Hypothesis, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright, bandit, pip-audit, OpenAPI generation.
  • Hardware: no physical sensors required — simulated smartwatch and dosimeter feeds, with an architecture ready for real wearables.

What makes it creative

  • A deterministic companion instead of an LLM — safer, offline, reproducible, and immune to prompt injection (input guards reject injected instructions).
  • A Link Simulator as a first-class feature, making communication loss testable rather than hidden.
  • An attack simulator with eight scenarios (forged signatures, replay, spoofed devices, tampered transit, timestamp manipulation, fake radiation spikes, false all-clears, flatline faults) plus benign controls.
  • Scenario evaluation with lead time and false-alarm metrics across normal, sleep degradation, radiation spike, gravity transition, and sensor fault cases.
  • Radiation treated honestly — dosimeters measure dose; later symptoms are described as co-occurring, never as proven causation.

Factors the team considered

Safety and scientific integrity came first: every value is simulated, thresholds are marked demo-only, and the product explicitly refuses to diagnose. The team designed for offline-first operation, communication delay, sensor unreliability, consent tiers, data minimization, raw-audio privacy, accessibility, Arabic/English support, and STRIDE-modeled threats. Validation currently covers 96 Python/Companion tests, 21 shared UI tests, typechecking, both production builds, and Playwright smoke tests, including an end-to-end pass where check-ins reached the Ground Station.
